added_claim_errors: "K-12 tuition (up to $10,000 a year)" is outdated: since January 1, 2026 the federal cap is $20,000 per beneficiary (checked on the web via several 529 provider pages and J.P. Morgan).

"Complete the transfer by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 limit" presents December 31 as the deadline. A rollover designated for 2026 can run to April 15, 2027, though plans vary. Minor error per the key.
"Some plans take two to four weeks" is unverifiable. Processing times vary by plan.
"The contributions themselves can be withdrawn tax-free at any time" for rolled-over money is not verified. The key lists the Roth ordering rules as not verified.
The Sources list (IRS newsroom, Savingforcollege, T. Rowe Price) gives links, so it is checkable. I did not open the Savingforcollege or T. Rowe Price pages.

"There is no separate December 31 deadline for the rollover itself; if you miss it, it becomes a 2027 rollover" is wrong or confusing. A 2026-designated rollover can be made through April 15, 2027, though plans vary. Minor error per the key.

The state survey is unverifiable. It claims "30 states follow federal", lists Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Utah and Vermont as recapturing deductions, and says Colorado, Missouri and New Jersey are "still deciding". It rests on one secondary source (praetorianguard.biz). The key did not check other states.

"California taxes the earnings plus a 2.5% penalty" is one accepted reading. The key calls whether California taxes the whole rollover or only the earnings unresolved, and the answer states it as settled.
"The excess is a nonqualified withdrawal, tax and 10% penalty on the earnings" is incomplete. It omits the 6% excise tax on the Roth side for excess contributions.
"Submit by early November. Processing can take several weeks" is unverifiable. Timing varies by plan.

The S. 5550 claim (introduced September 24, 2026, referred to Finance, would eliminate the aggregate rollover limit) is correct. I opened the govinfo link. The bill text does not state the $35,000 figure, but the claim is fair.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start: $7,500 for 2026, a $35,000 lifetime cap, so $13,000 can never go in. Both also cover the compensation limit, the direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into the son's own Roth, the 5-year and 15-year tests, income limits not applying, and a state-tax caveat. Both say December 31 is the cutoff for the 2026 limit, which is a minor error, because a 2026 rollover can be designated through April 15, 2027. A gives the full 2026-2030 schedule ($7,500 x 4, then $5,000), which B does not, but A never says what happens if the whole $48,000 goes in, and it repeats an outdated $10,000 K-12 cap that is $20,000 from 2026. B at least says the excess becomes a nonqualified withdrawal (though it omits the 6% Roth excise tax), is tighter, and its S. 5550 caveat checks out. B's detailed state list rests on one secondary source and cannot be verified. Overall it is close, and B's slight edge comes from no confirmed factual error, more concise delivery, and partial coverage of the over-contribution consequence.
